findings.subject: summary
findings.message: Read 3 of 4 files in 2 folders: 1 notebook (4 code cells), 1 Python script, 0 R scripts. Languages: Python. Dependencies: requirements.txt 4 requirements (0 pinned). The code reads 2 relative data paths; random numbers are drawn on 2 lines and a seed is set on 0 lines.
findings.fix: Nothing to fix; this is what the tool read. A clean report means none of the checks found anything, not that the result reproduces.

basis.text: At The Turing Way, we define reproducible research as work that can be independently recreated from the same data and the same code that the original team used.

findings.subject: README
findings.message: The folder has no README at its top level, so a reader does not learn what the study is, how to set up its environment, where the data comes from, or in what order to run the code.
findings.fix: Add a README.md that says what the study does, how to install the environment, where to get the data, and which scripts or notebooks to run in which order.

basis.text: For research to be reproducible, researchers must publish and distribute the entire contained analysis, not just its results.
If the project environment is not captured and the researchers need to return to their project after months or years (as is common in research), they will be unable to do so confidently.

findings.subject: LICENSE
findings.message: The folder has no LICENSE, LICENCE or COPYING file at its top level. Without one, others may read the code but have no permission to run, change or share it.
findings.fix: Add a LICENSE file with the license you choose for the code, and say in the README which terms cover the data.

basis.text: For research to be reproducible, researchers must publish and distribute the entire contained analysis, not just its results.

findings.subject: CITATION.cff
findings.message: The folder has no CITATION.cff, so there is no file that tells others how to cite the work.
findings.fix: Add a CITATION.cff with at least cff-version, message, title and authors. Code hosting sites and archives read it and show the citation.

findings.subject: requirements.txt
findings.message: 4 of 4 requirements in requirements.txt are not pinned to one version: pandas (no version), numpy (>=1.21), matplotlib (no version) and scikit-learn (~=1.3). pip installs the newest version that matches each one, so the same file gives other versions on another day, and there is no lock file that records the versions you used.
findings.fix: Pin each requirement to the version you ran the study with (pandas==2.1.4), for example from pip freeze in that environment, or commit a lock file (poetry.lock, uv.lock or Pipfile.lock) next to the ranges.

basis.text: When multiple candidate versions match a version specifier, the preferred version SHOULD be the latest version as determined by the consistent ordering defined by the standard Version scheme.
The strict version comparison operator is intended primarily for use when defining dependencies for repeatable deployments of applications while using a shared distribution index.

findings.subject: analysis.ipynb
findings.message: The code cells were not run once from top to bottom: the first run cell (cell 2) has execution count 3, so 2 runs are not in the saved notebook; cell 3 has execution count 1, after cell 2 with 3; cell 4 was not run, but cells before and after it were; the execution count jumps from 1 (cell 3) to 7 (cell 5). The saved execution counts in cell order are 3, 1, none, 7. Someone who runs the notebook from the top does not repeat what was run, so the outputs may not come back.
findings.fix: Restart the kernel and run all cells from the top (Restart Kernel and Run All Cells), check that the results are the same, and save the notebook again.

basis.text: They also have an execution_count, which must be an integer or null.
A result is reproducible when the same analysis steps performed on the same dataset consistently produces the same answer.

findings.subject: analysis.ipynb
findings.message: 1 cell of the notebook has a saved error: cell 5 (KeyError: 'wage'). The run that made the saved outputs did not finish cleanly, so later cells may rest on a state the code does not make.
findings.fix: Fix the cell or remove it, then restart the kernel, run all cells and save. If the error is the point of the cell, say so in a Markdown cell above it.

findings.subject: data/raw/responses_v2.csv
findings.message: pd.read_csv("data/raw/responses_v2.csv") at line 7 reads data/raw/responses_v2.csv, which is not in the folder and is not named in a README or data document.
findings.fix: Add the file to the folder, or say in the README where to get it (an address, and a version or checksum), or add a script that downloads it.

basis.text: At The Turing Way, we define reproducible research as work that can be independently recreated from the same data and the same code that the original team used.
Together with all other components of a research project, data identified in precise versions is part of the research outcome.

findings.subject: /home/mira/projects/survey/codebook.xlsx
findings.message: "/home/mira/projects/survey/codebook.xlsx" is a path in the home folder of one user. On another computer, or for another user, the path does not exist, so the code stops there.
findings.fix: Use a path relative to the folder of the study (data/codebook.xlsx), built from the place of the script (Path(__file__).parent in Python, here::here() in R), or read the folder from a setting.

basis.text: In essence, mobility of compute means being able to contain the entire software stack, from data files up through the library stack, and reliably move it from system to system.
Any research that is limited to where it can be deployed is instantly limited in the extent that it can be reproduced.

findings.subject: seed
findings.message: The code draws random numbers (analysis.ipynb cell 3: noise = np.random.normal(0, 1, len(df)) and clean_data.py line 12: random.shuffle(ids)) and no seed is set anywhere in the folder. Each run gives other numbers, so results that rest on them change from run to run.
findings.fix: Set a seed once at the top of each script or notebook: random.seed(42), np.random.seed(42) or rng = np.random.default_rng(42), torch.manual_seed(42), or set.seed(42) in R. Pass random_state to scikit-learn calls.

basis.text: A result is reproducible when the same analysis steps performed on the same dataset consistently produces the same answer.
Worse, some bugs may remain undetected, potentially impacting the results.

findings.subject: assigned-secret
findings.message: A key, token or password is written in the code: demo... (23 characters). Anyone who gets the folder gets the key, and it stays in the history of the repository after it is deleted.
findings.fix: Revoke the key now. Read it from an environment variable or a file that is not shared, clear the outputs that show it, and remove it from the history of the repository.

basis.text: You can now store sensitive data (tokens, keys, etc.) in environment variables and only specify the variable name for your requirements, letting pip lookup the value at runtime.

The Turing Way recognises that some research will use sensitive data that cannot be shared and this handbook will provide guides on how your research can be reproducible without all parts necessarily being open.
